title: Tabitha, arise (Acts 9:36–42)
hook: the widows show Peter the coats she made them
carry: she was full of good works

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananias, afraid, walking down the street called Straight. Your line was brother Saul.

An upstairs room in Joppa, a port town on the coast. A woman has died, and her body has been washed and laid out. The room is full of widows, crying. When Peter arrives, they don't make speeches about her. They hold up their clothes: coats, tunics, garments, all made by her hands. This one she sewed for me. This one too. It's a eulogy made of fabric. A sweater someone knitted, a quilt a grandmother made: some things keep a person close.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM IN JOPPA.` → `THE WIDOWS ARE WEEPING.` → `A EULOGY MADE OF FABRIC.`

segments.voice: Her name was Tabitha. Luke translates it for his Greek readers: Dorcas. Both names mean gazelle. And Luke calls her, plainly, a disciple, using the feminine form of the word. The Douay-Rheims sums up her life in one line: "This woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did." Not full of opinions, or plans. Full of works. When she falls sick and dies, the disciples hear that Peter is in Lydda, close by, and send two men: please come without delay. He comes, and the widows show him the coats and garments she made while she was with them. Then Peter does something that echoes a scene he once watched. He sends everyone out of the room, kneels, and prays. He turns to the body and says, "Tabitha, arise." She opens her eyes, sees Peter, and sits up. He gives her his hand, lifts her, and calls the saints and the widows to see her alive. Years before, Peter stood in a room where Jesus took a dead girl by the hand and said, in Aramaic, talitha cumi: little girl, arise. Talitha and Tabitha are one letter apart. Whether Luke meant the echo or not, Peter is doing what he saw his teacher do. And notice why the town cared so much: not because she was powerful, but because she clothed people nobody else clothed. Later, church sewing circles that made clothes for the poor were often called Dorcas societies, after her.
screen: `TABITHA, DORCAS: GAZELLE.` · `FULL OF GOOD WORKS.` · `THE COATS SHE MADE THEM.` · `PETER KNEELS AND PRAYS.` · then, large: `TABITHA, ARISE.`

segments.voice: Think of what your hands can make; not everyone sews, so maybe you cook, or fix bikes, or write, or fold a really good paper crane. Picture one person who could use something made by you and not bought, a note in your own handwriting, a meal, and picture handing it to them. If you pray, offer your hands for the day.
Tabitha. Dorcas, the gazelle of Joppa, a disciple whose good works were coats on widows' backs, raised when Peter said arise. Today's word.
Your line: she was full of good works. Her eulogy was the coats on the widows' backs. Day five hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Many Catholic parishes keep groups that sew, knit or cook for the poor, the sick and new mothers, and Tabitha is honored as a saint, traditionally on October 25.

original.note: Greek: gazelle, the meaning of the Aramaic name Tabitha. Luke gives both.

trapdoor: what you thought: another miracle story, Peter raising someone.
what it means: a town grieves a woman because she clothed the widows nobody clothed, and Peter does what he saw Jesus do.
what a scholar hears: scholars note that mathētria, a woman disciple, is used of no one else in the New Testament. and Peter's words to her sit one letter from Jesus' talitha cumi in Mark 5.

chat.says: Why did the widows show Peter all those coats after Tabitha died?
options: She had made them. Her life was full of good works, and the coats showed who she was.
They were selling her clothes to pay Peter for coming all the way from Lydda.
They wanted Peter to bless the coats so she could be buried in one of them.
chat.meaning: Tabitha was full of good works and almsdeeds. The widows held up the coats she had sewn for them: a eulogy made of fabric.

Joppa.meaning: a port town on the coast

Dorcas.meaning: Tabitha's name in Greek; both mean gazelle

Lydda.meaning: a town close by, where Peter was

almsdeeds.meaning: old word for acts of giving to the poor

talitha cumi.meaning: Aramaic: little girl, arise; Jesus's words to a dead girl

sources.quoted: This woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.

notes: Confirm the Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 9:36 and 9:40.
Tabitha as the only woman called mathētria in the New Testament: standard observation; confirm.
Dorcas societies in the 19th century: confirm phrasing.
Feast of Saint Tabitha traditionally October 25 in the Roman Martyrology; confirm.
Peter's presence at the raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:37) supports 'a scene he once watched'.
